rq_with_context: There are over 70 million grandparents in the U.S., and their roles are evolving as they live longer and engage more actively with grandchildren. Despite this, links between grandparent role expectations, communication patterns, and relationship satisfaction remain understudied. Prior research identifies two broad grandparent role types—guardians (authority-focused) and friends (supportive, fun-oriented)—and Family Communication Patterns Theory (FCPT) emphasizes conversation and conformity orientations as key dimensions shaping family dynamics. This study fills a gap by examining how these role expectations connect to FCPT dimensions and relational satisfaction from the grandparent perspective. Using survey data from 380 U.S. grandparents, it tests whether conversation and conformity orientations mediate the relationship between role expectations and satisfaction with both grandchild and adult child relationships. The study contributes by extending FCPT to grandparenting and showing how relational schemas influence communication and outcomes.

title: Projection Bias and Youth’s and Parents’ Perceptions of Their Joint Political Discussions
rq_with_context: Research on political socialization assumes that youth’s political development is influenced by family political discussions, but findings show only weak agreement between youth and parents about the frequency of these discussions. This study investigates whether this discrepancy stems from projection bias—where individuals project their own political interest onto their perceptions of family political interactions. The research asks whether youth’s and parents’ perceptions of political discussions and support are primarily driven by their own political interest, resulting in only limited correspondence between their reports. Using multivariate multiple regression analyses with two adolescent-parent cohorts (13- and 16-year-olds), the study tests this projection hypothesis. It contributes by explaining discrepancies in youth-parent reports and questioning the reliability of relying solely on one party’s account in political socialization research.

title: Associations between Parents’ Negative Talk about Aging and Young Adults’ Negative Affect and Efficacy Related to Aging
rq_with_context: Negative views of aging can harm physical health and longevity, yet little research has examined how family communication shapes young adults' beliefs about aging. While family members are a primary source of exposure to older adults and messages about aging, the specific role of parental talk remains understudied. This study investigates whether the frequency of parents' negative talk about aging (i.e., complaints and age excuses) is associated with young adults’ negative affect and aging-related efficacy. It also considers how a family’s general communication climate—specifically conversation orientation—influences these associations. Using survey data from college students, the study tests hypotheses derived from the communicative ecology model of successful aging, aiming to identify social communicative factors that shape young adults’ attitudes toward their own future aging.

title: Lesbian, Gay, and Heterosexual Parents’ Perspectives on Their Adopted Children’s Puberty and Approaches to Puberty-Related Communication
rq_with_context: Adoptive parents face unique challenges during their children’s transition to puberty because they lack genetic knowledge about pubertal timing and physical development, creating uncertainty. Parents in same-sex relationships may feel especially unprepared when parenting a different-sex child. Despite research on adolescence in adoptive and same-sex parent families, little is known about how these families navigate puberty specifically, especially in terms of communication. This study investigates how lesbian, gay, and heterosexual adoptive parents manage uncertainty and communicate about puberty with their adopted children. Using interviews with 60 parents of children aged 11–14, it explores how adoptive status, family structure, and child characteristics shape these experiences. The study applies uncertainty management theory, communicative openness, and queer theory to analyze responses. It contributes by illuminating how adoptive parents navigate a developmentally critical yet understudied transition, particularly across diverse family forms.

title: Attributions and Framing in Working Mothers’ Reports About Division of Family Labor
rq_with_context: The division of family labor remains a persistent source of inequity in dual earning families, particularly for working mothers who often carry a disproportionate share of visible and invisible tasks. While prior research has highlighted structural and cultural factors influencing this imbalance, less is known about how mothers communicatively make sense of these divisions. This study addresses that gap by exploring the attributions and self/other framings mothers use when reflecting on family labor. Using communicated sense-making theory, the authors analyzed open-ended survey responses from 34 working mothers. The central research questions are: (1) What reasons do mothers in dual earning families give for their division of family labor? and (2) How do mothers frame themselves and their partners in these attributions? The study identifies key attributions across external, relational, and internal factors and reveals patterns of negative self- and partner-framing that may influence relational well-being.

title: Whose Family Communication Counts? Investigating the Validity of the Revised Family Communication Patterns Scale Across Racial Groups
rq_with_context: The Revised Family Communication Patterns (RFCP) scale is a foundational instrument in family communication research, yet its application has largely relied on homogenous, White samples. Given increasing calls for inclusive scholarship and known cultural differences in family communication, this study examines the measurement validity of the RFCP across four major racial groups in the US: Hispanic, Asian, Black, and White. While prior research has established the scale's utility, little is known about whether its subscales function equivalently across racially diverse populations. The study poses the central question: Is the RFCP scale valid across different racial groups in assessing family communication patterns? Using measurement invariance testing with a stratified sample (N = 644), the study evaluates whether the factor structure of the RFCP—specifically its conversation and conformity orientation subscales—is consistent across groups. A key contribution lies in testing the instrument’s cross-group reliability, offering guidance for future research on diversity in family communication.

title: “Wake up, Boo”: race and the performance of wokeness inBig Brother 22
rq_with_context: Big Brother 22 aired during a heightened racial justice moment in 2020, amidst widespread calls for awareness and anti-racism. This essay investigates how the reality show responded by incorporating visible performances of wokeness—such as conversations about racial injustice and acts of allyship—marking a shift from its post-racial roots. Yet, despite these efforts, a white male emerged as the winner, indicating the persistence of racial status quo. The gap addressed is how media can appear progressive while still reinforcing dominant racial structures. Using critical cultural analysis, the study examines episodes, producer decisions, and contestant interactions to understand the dual function of 'Woke TV.' The contribution lies in showing how reality television performs wokeness through microreparations and allyship, even as systemic inequities remain unchallenged.

title: Public deliberation and social justice sensibilities in Greensboro Participatory Budgeting
rq_with_context: Participatory budgeting (PB) has been promoted as a democratic tool to empower marginalized communities and advance social justice, yet its ability to do so—especially in the U.S.—remains contested. While public deliberation scholars debate the roles of equity, activism, and justice in deliberative processes, PB uniquely combines deliberation with direct decision-making power over public funds. This study investigates how the inaugural PB process in Greensboro, NC, a grassroots-led initiative, fostered or hindered social justice sensibilities among participants. Drawing on Iris Marion Young’s theory of communicative democracy, the authors analyze qualitative data from participant observations and interviews to understand how concerns about power, equity, and fairness were expressed in residents’ talk. The research contributes an empirical account of how everyday communication in PB can reflect and cultivate a social justice orientation, even when institutional actors resist transformative outcomes.

title: The interaction of evolving media structure and life-course dynamics: the changing landscape of media use in China (2005–2015)
rq_with_context: Media use in China has shifted dramatically since the 2000s, with Internet use rising and traditional media declining, yet little is known about the underlying mechanisms driving these changes. Existing research often conflates age, period, and cohort effects or relies on single-time surveys, making it difficult to isolate the drivers of media-use change. Using three waves of the China General Social Survey (2005–2015), this study applies age-period-cohort (APC) analysis to disentangle these temporal effects and track how Internet use impacts television and newspaper use across cohorts. The research questions are: (1) How has media use changed in China from 2005 to 2015? and (2) How has Internet use affected traditional media use among different cohorts? By combining APC modeling and hierarchical regression, the study reveals how media habits formed in youth persist, yet are adjusted based on period-level media shifts and life-course stages. It contributes to understanding the coexistence of generational persistence and dynamic adjustment in media use within a rapidly transforming media environment.

title: Digital propaganda, political bots and polarized politics in India
rq_with_context: Digital propaganda through political bots has become a growing concern in democracies, especially during crises and elections. While existing research has documented bot activity in Western contexts, less is known about their role in developing countries like India, where internet penetration is expanding rapidly but asymmetrically. This study addresses the gap by investigating how automated and semi-automated Twitter accounts shaped public opinion during the 2016 Uri attack and Surgical Strike. Using Twitter data and critical discourse analysis, the paper asks whether a small number of accounts, many later suspended, manipulated the online conversation. It draws on hybrid media theory and applies detection methods from prior computational studies. The key contribution is empirical evidence of digital propaganda in India and a call for integrating computational and critical methods to understand bot influence.

title: Falling for fake news: the role of political bias and cognitive ability
rq_with_context: The spread of fake news online has raised concerns due to its impacts on public understanding and democratic processes. While research has separately examined cognitive ability, political bias, and media use, few studies have integrated these factors. This study addresses that gap by testing a model that combines cognitive ability and political bias as predictors of fake news belief, with news consumption patterns as mediating pathways. Using a nationally representative survey of 855 social media users in Singapore, the study applies dual process theory to understand how individuals process information. It finds that both cognitive ability and political bias significantly predict belief in fake news, both directly and indirectly through their influence on media use. The contribution lies in demonstrating how individual differences interact with media behaviors to shape susceptibility to misinformation.

title: Expert-Informed Topic Models for Document Set Discovery
rq_with_context: Many text-as-data studies require identifying documents that discuss a broad thematic area (e.g., religion in public life) within large, unstructured corpora. However, standard keyword approaches risk selection bias, especially when researchers lack domain knowledge. Current methods like King et al.’s keyword-assisted algorithm still depend on researchers’ ability to judge relevant keywords, which is problematic in cross-national or unfamiliar contexts. This paper proposes expert-informed topic models (EITM) as a solution, combining expert survey inputs with LDA topic modeling to discover thematically relevant documents. The research question is whether EITM can more validly and efficiently identify relevant documents than keyword-based searches. The approach uses a seven-step workflow involving expert elicitation, topic modeling, and relevance scoring. The authors claim a contribution by providing a validated, flexible method that reduces selection bias and supports researcher learning in unfamiliar contexts.

title: What’s in a name? The effect of named entities on topic modelling interpretability
rq_with_context: Topic modeling is widely used in communication and social sciences to uncover latent themes in large text corpora. However, while preprocessing choices like stopword removal are known to influence results, the impact of named entity (NE) handling remains understudied. Despite NEs carrying contextual meaning, their presence may bias topic formation by linking actors to issues or dominating topic word lists. This paper addresses the gap by asking how retaining or removing NEs affects topic model interpretability. Using the Newsroom dataset and LDA-based models, the authors compare models trained on versions of the same corpus—with and without NEs—using both model performance metrics (coherence, exclusivity) and human validation from expert and crowd coders. The key contribution is empirical evidence that NE removal systematically improves perceived model interpretability, despite NEs being more prevalent in top topic words than expected by chance.

title: Building an ICCN Multimodal Classifier of Aggressive Political Debate Style: Towards a Computational Understanding of Candidate Performance Over Time
rq_with_context: Political debates have evolved toward more aggressive, confrontational styles, especially evident in recent U.S. elections. While prior research analyzes verbal, nonverbal, or tonal cues in isolation, this study addresses the gap in understanding how these modalities work together to signal aggression. The authors ask whether a novel Interaction Canonical Correlation Network (ICCN) classifier, trained on human-coded 10-second debate segments from 1980 to 2020, can accurately detect multimodal aggression. Using a longitudinal multimodal dataset, they compare unimodal and multimodal classification performance, particularly before and after 2016. The work contributes a computational tool for scalable, fine-grained analysis of candidate behavior over time.

title: Comparing Chatbots and Online Surveys for (Longitudinal) Data Collection: An Investigation of Response Characteristics, Data Quality, and User Evaluation
rq_with_context: As chatbots become more prevalent in communication research, they are increasingly considered as tools for survey administration. While prior studies suggest chatbots may improve engagement and data quality due to their conversational nature, empirical evidence comparing them directly with web surveys—especially over time—is limited. There is a gap in understanding whether chatbots offer methodological advantages in response characteristics, data quality, and user experience compared to established web survey methods. This study addresses this by conducting a longitudinal, pre-registered experiment (N=304) comparing a chatbot survey (via Skype) with a web survey (via Qualtrics) over 14 days. The research investigates differences in response rates, response times, open-response length, internal consistency, attention check performance, and variability. It also explores how these metrics change over time and how users evaluate each mode in terms of perceived usefulness, enjoyment, security, and cognitive effort. The study contributes methodological insights into whether chatbots can be valid alternatives to traditional web surveys.

title: JST and rJST: joint estimation of sentiment and topics in textual data using a semi-supervised approach
rq_with_context: Automated sentiment analysis is widely used in political communication research, but common methods like sentiment dictionaries assume word valence is fixed, ignoring how meaning changes with context. This domain-specificity problem limits cross-context comparability. While transformer models address this via contextual embeddings, they require substantial resources and data. JST and rJST offer a middle-ground approach by jointly modeling sentiment and topics within a bag-of-words framework, allowing sentiment to vary by topic. Despite their potential, these models have not been evaluated or used in political communication research. This paper asks how well JST and rJST perform in estimating both overall and topic-specific sentiment in legislative speeches across three languages, compared to established methods including dictionaries, embedding-enhanced approaches, Latent Semantic Scaling, and GPT-4. The study uses human-coded sentiment as a benchmark and assesses both concurrent and predictive validity. The authors argue that even if outperformed by transformers, JST and rJST are valuable due to their transparency, low resource needs, and ability to produce interpretable, topic-conditioned sentiment.

title: High Expectations, Hostile Perception, and Biased Coverage? The Labour Movement and the Press Coverage of the Paris Commune, 1871
rq_with_context: The socialist labour movement in the nineteenth century viewed the bourgeois press as hostile and biased, despite attaching high expectations to journalistic norms like objectivity and fairness. This paper investigates whether these perceptions corresponded to actual media bias during the coverage of the Paris Commune in 1871, a key moment for the labour movement. Drawing on the concepts of hostile media perception and media bias, it analyzes 1,092 articles from The Times and Kölnische Zeitung. While the movement claimed marginalization and partisan reporting, the study reveals that coverage was largely neutral in tone and did include voices from the Commune, though to a limited extent. The gap between perception and content suggests that even relatively neutral reporting can be perceived as biased when measured against emerging professional norms.

title: Respawning the Hero: Metapolitics, Historical Fiction Video Games and the Shifting Strategies and Subjectivities of Far-right Influencers
rq_with_context: Far-right influencers increasingly use historical fiction video games to promote reactionary cultural imaginaries tied to mythic pasts, racial purity, and civilisational struggle. While prior research has linked far-right politics to gamer culture and backlash, less is known about how the specific affordances and constraints of games shape ideological discourse. This article addresses that gap by analyzing how influencers negotiate moments when game mechanics or representations disrupt their desired historical narratives. Drawing on multimodal critical discourse analysis of Let’s Play videos and video essays, it explores how influencers shift subject positions—between heroic embodiment, historical truth-telling, and cultural grievance—to maintain ideological coherence. The approach integrates game studies and discourse theory to show how platformed gameplay becomes a site of metapolitical performance. The key contribution is revealing how ideological discourse adapts dynamically to structural constraints in ludic environments.

title: Role of Emotions in Protest Participants’ Perception of Radical Performances: The Case of Gezi Protests in Turkey
rq_with_context: Mass protests like the 2013 Gezi protests in Turkey bring together diverse groups with varying political and cultural backgrounds, leading to differing judgments about what constitutes appropriate or radical behavior. While existing research has explored public perceptions of protest repertoires, there is limited understanding of how participants internally evaluate radical performances—such as violent acts, controversial slogans, or identity displays—especially within heterogeneous movements. This paper fills that gap by analyzing 17 in-depth interviews with Gezi protesters to understand how emotions inform these evaluations. The central research question is how emotions influence protesters’ definitions and perceptions of radical performances during contention. Using constructivist grounded theory, the study identifies three key emotional dimensions: emotions toward the protest, emotions toward the actors involved, and emotions toward the performance itself. The findings contribute to social movement scholarship by revealing the emotional underpinnings of how participants assess radicalism, highlighting that perception is not solely based on legality or ideology, but deeply shaped by affective and moral judgments.

title: How do English-Speaking Users Discuss the Wuhan Lockdown: A Longitudinal Analysis of Public Spheres on YouTube
rq_with_context: The study investigates how English-speaking YouTube users engaged with the Wuhan lockdown—a pivotal early event of the COVID-19 pandemic—across two discussion waves in 2020. While early debates occurred when the crisis was largely confined to China, a second wave emerged as the pandemic spread to the West, raising questions about how changing local contexts influence global discourse. The authors identify a gap in idealized notions of a rational, universal public sphere, which often overlook affective, transient, and context-dependent online debates. Drawing on Mouffe, Bakhtin, and Butler, they analyze sentiment and comment topics across major media outlets (e.g., BBC, CGTN, CNN) to understand how emotions and concerns evolved. They test three hypotheses regarding the impact of pandemic severity, local context, and media environment on user discussions. The study contributes by showing that global publics are not universal but fluid, affective, and shaped by immediate sociopolitical conditions.

title: Visual, Popular and Political: The Non-profit Influencer and the Public Sphere
rq_with_context: The rise of social media influencers has predominantly been studied through the lens of commercial branding and self-promotion. However, a growing number of influencers engage with societal and political issues, operating outside profit-driven motives. This study focuses on 'non-profit influencers' in Norway—individuals with large followings who address public concerns such as gender equality and moral accountability. The gap lies in understanding how their rhetoric functions in democratic public discourse, beyond traditional politics and market logic. Guided by the research question—what rhetorical building blocks do non-profit influencers use, and how does their communication inform our understanding of popular figures in the public sphere?—the study conducts a multimodal rhetorical analysis of Instagram posts by two such influencers. Drawing on cultural public sphere theory and argumentation frameworks, it identifies key rhetorical tools and situates them within broader democratic communication. The contribution is an empirical demonstration of how informal, visually driven, normatively oriented communication can stimulate public deliberation in digitally mediated environments.

title: Electronic Surveillance and Australian Journalism: Surveillance Normalization and EmergentNorms of Information Security
rq_with_context: Journalism in democratic societies relies on secure communication between reporters and sources, especially whistleblowers exposing wrongdoing. In Australia, a series of surveillance laws enacted since 2015—including the metadata retention scheme and the Assistance and Access Act—have significantly expanded state surveillance powers. While existing research highlights global threats to source protection, less is known about how these specific legal changes shape journalistic practice in Australia. This study investigates how Australian journalists perceive and respond to these laws, particularly regarding source protection and information security. Using interviews with 19 journalists and two media lawyers, the paper explores the gap between legal safeguards and journalists' trust in them. It finds that despite no major editorial self-censorship, sources are withdrawing due to surveillance fears, and journalists are increasingly adopting information security measures. The core contribution is showing how surveillance normalization coexists with an emergent norm of information security awareness among journalists.

title: An Ecosystem of Collective Futures: How Journalists and Experts Co-Construct Projections in Hybrid Media Environments
rq_with_context: During crises like the COVID-19 pandemic, journalists and experts play key roles in communicating risks and future scenarios, but hybrid media environments have transformed how such knowledge is produced. Traditional models of journalistic mediation, where journalists transform expert knowledge into news, are challenged by multi-directional, platform-bridging interactions. Existing research relies heavily on interview and network methods, leaving the textual and discursive practices of co-constructed projections underexplored. This study addresses that gap by analyzing how journalists and experts co-construct pandemic-related projections across news and social media. Using qualitative textual analysis of 400 projections in the U.S. and Israel, it introduces the concept of 'predictive agency' to examine who participates in shaping future claims. The authors aim to reveal how collective futures are negotiated, and how accountability is distributed across actors in hybrid systems.

title: This Isn’t Journalism, It’s Propaganda! Patterns of News Media Bias Accusations on Twitter, 2010–2020
rq_with_context: In many democracies, mainstream news media are increasingly criticized as politically biased, particularly by right-leaning actors, despite systematic evidence showing no such bias. In Sweden, despite a politically independent media system with no demonstrable bias, a significant trust gap exists between left- and right-leaning audiences. This paper addresses the under-researched role of social media—specifically Twitter—in amplifying political bias accusations against news media. It investigates the prevalence and targets of such accusations over time, their political origins, and how they are discursively constructed. Using a mixed-methods CADS approach, the study analyzes 167,527 Swedish tweets to document patterns of media bias discourse. The key contribution is revealing the dominance of right-wing populist voices in shaping media criticism, turning it into a core element of political identity rather than journalistic accountability.

title: What Does a Journalist Look like? Visualizing Journalistic Roles through AI
rq_with_context: The study explores how AI-generated images reflect societal perceptions of journalists, focusing on the visual dimension of the 'who is a journalist?' debate. While prior research has examined popular culture depictions, AI-generated imagery remains underexplored despite its growing influence in media. The authors identify a gap in understanding how algorithmic systems represent journalistic roles and whether these representations reinforce or disrupt existing biases. Using Midjourney, they generate images from generic and specialized journalistic terms to analyze patterns in gender, appearance, and technology use. They apply visual social semiotics to interpret how these images construct journalistic identity. The study contributes by revealing how AI visualizations perpetuate stereotypes related to gender, age, and race in journalism roles.

title: The Relevance of Digital News: Themes, Scales and Temporalities
rq_with_context: The phenomenon of news relevance has traditionally been defined by journalists, but recent research highlights a disconnect between journalistic and audience perceptions. Despite growing interest in audience-centered news relevance, the concept remains undertheorized and often confined to traditional news journalism. This study addresses the gap by investigating how young Swedish adults construct news relevance in digital environments, where news is understood more broadly than journalism. Drawing on phenomenological theory and empirical interview data, the research asks: How do young audiences determine what digital news is relevant? It uses a radical user perspective and abductive analysis to explore relevance as an everyday practice. The paper contributes a new matrix of four types of news relevance and a theoretical definition grounded in themes, scales, and temporalities.

title: Boosting or Limiting? Examining How FoMO Influences Personal News Curation Through News Fatigue in Social Media
rq_with_context: People increasingly curate their news on social media, actively shaping what they see through actions like following, liking, blocking, or unfollowing. While prior research has explored the curated flows framework, it largely ignores the psychological mechanisms driving these behaviors. The affective drivers of personal news curation—particularly how Fear of Missing Out (FoMO) influences curation strategies—remain unclear. This study addresses this gap by examining whether FoMO boosts or limits news curation through social media news fatigue. Grounded in the Stress-Strain-Outcome (SSO) model, it tests how FoMO (stress) leads to news fatigue (strain), influencing news-boosting and news-limiting curation (outcomes). Using survey data from 1,198 Chinese social media users working from home, the study reveals how fatigue mediates these relationships.

title: Retrieving and Repurposing: A Grounded Approach to Hyperlocal Working Practices through a Subcultural Lens
rq_with_context: The decline of mainstream local journalism in the UK has created a space filled by independent hyperlocal operators, often positioned as grassroots, community-oriented alternatives. While existing research focuses on political economy and sustainability, less attention has been paid to the cultural dimensions of these practices. This paper addresses the gap by asking how hyperlocal operators, functioning as a news subculture, retrieve and repurpose mainstream practices in their work. Using subcultural theory and a grounded approach, the study analyzes interviews with 27 UK hyperlocal publishers. It reveals that their practices reflect bricolage—reusing and adapting elements like face-to-face journalism and print formats once common in legacy media. The authors claim this cultural lens offers a new framework for understanding hyperlocal media as a resistant yet adaptive subculture.

title: What News Users Perceive as ‘Alternative Media’ Varies between Countries: How Media Fragmentation and Polarization Matter
rq_with_context: Alternative media have traditionally been defined as corrective outlets opposing mainstream media, but recent changes in media environments challenge this distinction. While scholars have debated definitions of alternative media, little is known about how audiences perceive which sources are 'alternative.' This study addresses that gap by examining audience perceptions across five countries with varying levels of media fragmentation and polarization. The research asks whether users in more fragmented and polarized media environments differ in their identification of alternative media sources. Using survey data from Denmark, Italy, Poland, Switzerland, and the US, the study analyzes both self-perceived use of alternative media and the specific outlets users name as alternative. It contributes by showing that audience perceptions of alternativeness are shaped by macro-level media structures, revealing that structural features of media systems influence not just media content but also how audiences categorize media sources.

title: Benefits of Diverse News Recommendations for Democracy: A User Study
rq_with_context: News recommender systems shape public discourse by curating personalized content, often optimizing for user preferences, which may limit exposure to diverse viewpoints and reinforce political polarization. While prior research discusses the normative role of recommender systems in democratic contexts, little empirical evidence compares diversity-optimized recommendations to accuracy-based ones in real-world settings. This study addresses that gap by testing how diversity-aware algorithms affect user behavior and societal outcomes. Using a custom-built news app in a five-week experimental design with Swiss users, the authors compare chronological, accuracy-optimized, and diversity-optimized recommendations. They find that diverse recommendations perform similarly in user utility, increase tolerance for opposing views—especially among conservatives—and may nudge users toward preferring cross-cutting content. The study contributes by providing empirical evidence that diversity in news recommendations can yield societal benefits without sacrificing user satisfaction.

title: How Message Features and Social Endorsements Affect the Longevity of News Sharing
rq_with_context: News diffusion typically follows a lifecycle of growth, peak, and decline, but some stories remain shareable longer than others. While prior research has focused on the volume of news sharing, less is known about what drives its duration—especially how message content and social popularity cues interact. This study investigates the determinants of the longevity of audience news sharing, using behavioral data from New York Times health articles. It tests how message features (e.g., informational utility, emotional positivity) and social endorsements (e.g., time on the 'most-emailed' list) affect how long articles continue to be shared via email and social media, both separately and together. The approach uses event history analysis on population-level sharing data. The study claims to advance understanding of news virality by showing that both message content and social signals shape sharing duration, with synergistic effects when both are present.

title: “It’s in the Air”—Sponsored Editorial Content as a Path for Stealth Government Propaganda: The Case of Israeli Media
rq_with_context: The article investigates the rise of government-sponsored content (GSC) in Israeli digital journalism, a practice where government ministries fund media content presented as editorial while their sponsorship remains obscured. Despite formal prohibitions, GSC has flourished due to inconsistent regulation and political influence, creating a legal grey zone. Existing research has explored commercial branded content and native advertising but has not examined government actors as sponsors. This gap is critical because GSC poses unique threats when public funds are used for strategic messaging in media spaces. The study asks: (1) How are GSC agreements arranged under legally ambiguous conditions? and (2) How do these deals blur editorial and advertising boundaries? Using case studies of Israeli campaigns (2014–2017) and triangulated sources, the analysis applies Habermas’s theory of communicative action. It argues that GSC corrupts journalistic integrity by enabling stealth propaganda, and contributes empirical and theoretical insight into how state-sponsored content manipulates public discourse.

title: Understanding Customer Responses to AI-Driven Personalized Journeys: Impacts on the Customer Experience
rq_with_context: The digital customer journey is increasingly shaped by AI-driven personalization, yet existing research focuses more on technical capabilities than on experiential impacts. While prior work demonstrates how algorithms leverage data for recommendations across retail, social media, and e-commerce, it overlooks how these technologies affect broader journey experiences—particularly the balance between personalization and customer autonomy. This study addresses that gap by exploring customer perceptions of AI-driven touchpoints. It specifically investigates two research questions: how AI-driven algorithms influence brand engagement, and how they impact the tension between personalized content and consumer control. Using semi-structured phenomenological interviews and Customer Journey Mapping, the authors analyze experiences across multiple touchpoints. The study contributes by critically contextualizing AI in ethical debates around consumer autonomy and highlighting practitioner responsibilities in combining technological advances with user empowerment.

title: Boredom in the Creative Studio
rq_with_context: Boredom is a prevalent but understudied emotion in creative work settings, despite its negative effects on motivation and creativity. While prior research has explored boredom in lab or general workplace contexts, little is known about its causes and impacts in real-world creative industries, where personality and task identity may heighten susceptibility. This study addresses this gap by exploring how control and value appraisals—derived from control-value theory (CVT)—influence boredom among professional creatives. Based on interviews with over 30 agency professionals, it investigates the antecedents, consequences, and mitigation strategies for boredom. The research identifies poor briefing, lack of autonomy, insufficient feedback, repetition, and identity incongruence as key triggers, and reveals both individual (reduced effort) and social (asocial/antisocial) consequences. Its contribution lies in applying CVT to a naturalistic creative context and identifying client-related and identity-based factors previously unlinked to boredom.

title: More than Shapes: The Silhouette Effect in Advertising
rq_with_context: Despite the widespread use of silhouettes in advertising, little is known about their impact on consumers compared to attractive models. Existing research suggests that exposure to attractive models can trigger self-threat through social comparison, leading to negative ad responses. This study addresses the gap by investigating why silhouettes might be more effective, proposing that reduced appearance details lower self-threat. The research question is: under what conditions are silhouettes more effective than attractive models in advertising? The study uses multiple experiments to test the role of self-threat as a mechanism, with a focus on product type and appearance-related self-esteem as moderators. The work contributes by identifying the 'silhouette effect' and its boundary conditions.

title: Ad Agency Leadership in the US, UK, and Australia: A Mixed-Method Analysis of Effective Attributes and Styles
rq_with_context: Leadership in advertising agencies is understudied compared to other fields, despite agencies facing significant changes due to technology, competition from consulting firms, and evolving workforce expectations. While the GLOBE project has identified universal and culturally specific leadership attributes across 63 countries, its application to the creative advertising industry remains unexplored. This study addresses this gap by investigating what attributes and styles are seen as effective among advertising professionals in three Anglo-cluster countries—US, UK, and Australia—that share cultural similarities yet have unique identities. Using a mixed-method approach with surveys and interviews, the research asks: What leadership attributes and styles are viewed as most effective by agency professionals in these regions? The study applies GLOBE’s Culturally Endorsed Leadership Theory to analyze responses. It contributes by validating and extending leadership theory in a creative industry context and identifying industry-specific preferences, such as a stronger emphasis on collaboration and soft skills.

title: Sources of security risk information: What do professionals rely on for their risk assessment?
rq_with_context: Security risks stemming from malicious human actions often lack reliable historical data, making expert judgment the primary basis for risk assessment. Professionals in both physical and cybersecurity domains must therefore rely on various information sources to evaluate threats, yet little is known about which sources they use or how they assess their quality. Existing research has highlighted the importance of expert judgment and information reliability, but no prior study has systematically examined the range of sources used in practice or how their perceived quality compares to actual use. This study addresses this gap by identifying 17 potential sources, evaluating their perceived quality using the NATO intelligence evaluation system supplemented with a novel 'source intention' criterion, and comparing this quality ranking to actual usage patterns gathered from a survey of 174 professionals. The authors aim to understand how professionals form judgments and whether the most trusted sources are indeed the most used, contributing to more informed and conscious selection of information in risk management.

title: A nightmare to control: Legal and organizational challenges around the procurement of journalistic AI from external technology providers
rq_with_context: As media organizations increasingly adopt AI technologies, they face significant legal and operational challenges in procuring systems from external providers, particularly due to unequal bargaining power and opaque contractual terms. Existing research has focused on AI’s impact on journalistic practices but has largely overlooked the procurement phase, especially the negotiation of contractual conditions. This study addresses this gap by investigating professionals’ perceptions of the procurement process, the legal and practical barriers they encounter, and how media organizations can strengthen their position. Drawing on 12 semi-structured interviews with lawyers, technologists, and managers, and an analysis of 16 AI providers’ terms and conditions, the study uses a qualitative, interpretive approach grounded in the City of Amsterdam’s standard contractual clauses for AI procurement. It aims to propose a framework for contractual counter-power to support fairer negotiations, particularly for smaller and local media actors who are most vulnerable in these processes.

title: Internet appropriation barriers in the lives of Dutch parents living in poverty: A qualitative study
rq_with_context: As poverty and digital exclusion are closely linked, understanding the barriers that prevent parents in poverty from benefiting from internet opportunities is critical. While prior research identifies general barriers such as limited resources, low self-esteem, and poor digital skills among low-income populations, there is little empirical data on Dutch parents in poverty specifically. The study addresses two gaps: first, what internet appropriation barriers these parents face, and second, how these barriers connect to and affect different life domains—economic, social, cultural, and personal. Using a qualitative approach with 18 semi-structured interviews, the research applies Van Dijk’s internet appropriation model and Helsper’s corresponding fields model. The authors claim the study contributes by mapping detailed, real-life barriers and showing how life domains are interrelated in the context of digital exclusion.

title: Content creation and gig-work in the platform economy: What contemporary sex work can teach us about the futures of digital labor
rq_with_context: The paper addresses how digital sex work — particularly among adult entertainers on direct-to-consumer platforms like OnlyFans — problematizes standard conceptualizations of gig-work, which often emphasize anonymity, platform centralization, and fragmented labor. Existing research tends to treat gig-work as low-skilled and isolated from broader identity formation, failing to account for creative laborers who build cumulative personas across multiple platforms. This study asks how adult entertainers’ strategies for survival and success in a highly marginalized, algorithmically governed environment can inform broader understandings of digital labor. Using situational analysis of interviews and media practices, the research explores how these workers negotiate authenticity, emotional labor, and platform control. The key claimed contribution is a reconceptualization of gig-work that emphasizes dispersed professional identities, relational labor, and the cumulative nature of online content creation.

title: Trusting the untrustable: The construction of politicians’ self-image on Facebook
rq_with_context: Political candidates possess unobservable personal qualities that voters need to assess when making electoral decisions, yet traditional media often fail to convey this information, creating an information asymmetry. While existing research has explored political personalization on social media, few have considered this asymmetry as a central problem. Drawing on signaling theory, this study investigates how politicians reduce this gap by sending visible signals of their personal qualities via Facebook. The authors analyze semi-structured interviews with 12 Israeli female politicians and their Facebook posts to identify the tactics used. They propose a signaling model tailored to SNS political communication, focusing on index and costly signals. The study contributes to understanding how digital platforms reshape candidate-voter interactions by enabling direct signaling of trustworthiness.

title: Domesticating algorithms: An exploratory study of Facebook users in Myanmar
rq_with_context: In Myanmar, Facebook has become the primary gateway to the internet and news following rapid democratization and telecom reform. Despite extensive research on social media use, few studies examine how users in emerging markets interpret and interact with algorithms. There is a gap in understanding how people with limited prior digital experience make sense of algorithmically mediated environments. Drawing on domestication theory and algorithm studies, this exploratory study investigates how 18 Facebook users in Yangon perceive and use the Facebook algorithm. It explores how they incorporate algorithmic functionality—particularly through the 'Friends' feature—into daily information practices. The author argues that users believe adding strangers as 'Friends' funnels news into their feeds, thereby shaping their domestication process. The study contributes by revealing how algorithmic systems are interpreted and adapted in a specific sociocultural context.

title: La construcción mediática del colectivo LGTB+ en el cine blockbuster de Hollywood. El uso del pinkwashing  y el queerbaiting
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: Hollywood blockbusters, produced by major studios with large budgets and global reach, have recently promoted the inclusion of LGBT+ characters as a sign of progressiveness, responding to criticism from organizations like GLAAD about the lack of sexual diversity in mainstream cinema. However, GLAAD's 2018 report revealed that LGBT+ representation in blockbusters reached an all-time low in 2017, with most portrayals being brief and stereotypical. This study addresses the gap between promotional claims and actual on-screen representation. The research question is: Do Hollywood studios use pinkwashing and queerbaiting to create a false image of inclusivity without meaningfully integrating LGBT+ characters? To answer this, the authors analyze five major blockbusters using critical discourse analysis (CDA). The study contributes by exposing how marketing strategies mask ongoing exclusion and reinforce heteronormativity in popular cinema.

title: El papel de los medios de comunicación en situaciones de crisis sanitaria. La percepción de la población en torno al control y las normas sociales durante la pandemia del COVID-19
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: The study addresses how mass media shape public perception and behavior during health crises like the COVID-19 pandemic. While prior research highlights media's role in constructing social reality and promoting norm compliance, less is known about how individuals perceive media-driven social control and how this relates to actual normative behavior. Drawing on survey data from 704 people in Spain, the research explores the relationship between media perception and public willingness to abide by and enforce social norms. Using a quantitative approach with Likert-scale responses analyzed via SPSS, it investigates how age and sex influence these dynamics. The study contributes by showing that media perception is linked to social control behaviors, particularly among specific age and gender groups.

title: Sinergias de sororidad en las comunidades virtuales de las revistas femeninas. El caso del cierre  del foro de Vogue
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: The study investigates the unique female virtual community of the Vogue Spain forum, which was shut down in 2018 after fifteen years of operation. While forums on digital media are declining, this case is significant because the forum had evolved into an autonomous space for women’s interaction, largely independent from the magazine’s editorial agenda. Existing research has shown that online spaces often marginalize women's voices, yet this forum became a rare site of female-centered dialogue and solidarity. The closure—prompted by public accusations of cyber-bullying against influencer Lovely Pepa—raised questions about why the magazine chose to shut down the entire forum instead of addressing specific abusive content. Based on structured surveys with 47 former users, the research asks how this community functioned, what needs it fulfilled, and what dynamics of sorority emerged. Using qualitative analysis of user testimonies, the study highlights the emotional and practical support networks developed among women who used the forum to discuss motherhood, health, work, and personal crises. Its contribution lies in documenting a unique case of female digital community-building that challenged traditional media-audience relationships.

title: Centennials en TikTok: tipología de vídeos. Análisis y comparativa España-Gran Bretaña por género, edad y nacionalidad
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: TikTok has become a major social platform for teenagers, yet there is limited research on the types of content they produce, especially from a cross-national comparative perspective. While existing studies explore teen behavior on platforms like YouTube and Instagram, few analyze TikTok content quantitatively across different national and demographic groups. This study addresses this gap by analyzing 447 videos from 24 teen TikTok creators—12 from Spain and 12 from the UK—aged 11–17, all with over half a million followers. The research asks what types of videos Spanish and British teens upload, and whether gender, age, or nationality influences content type. Using content analysis, the authors classify videos into categories such as choreographies, video-selfies, and funny videos. They test for statistical associations between demographics and content, aiming to reveal patterns in teen digital expression and self-representation.

title: Las asociaciones de enfermedades raras: Estructura de sus redes e identificación de los líderes de opinión mediante la técnica del análisis de redes sociales
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: Social networks have become central to how health information is shared, particularly for rare diseases (RD), where patients and organizations rely on digital platforms to raise awareness, share support, and advocate for research. While previous studies have looked at media coverage and communication strategies of RD organizations, few have applied social network analysis (SNA) to understand the relational structures on platforms like Twitter. Existing work on social media influencers often relies on superficial metrics like follower counts, which do not capture real influence. This study addresses that gap by using SNA to map the networks around three major RD federations—FEDER (Spain), EURORDIS (Europe), and NORD (USA)—to uncover the true structure of influence beyond follower numbers. The research questions are: who are the key actors in these networks, what types of relationships form within them, and what topics dominate the conversations? The study uses NodeXL software to collect and visualize Twitter networks based on mentions and retweets. It contributes by identifying structural positions of influencers using centrality metrics, offering a more accurate picture of online influence in the rare disease community.

title: Curación de noticias en el correo electrónico: análisis de newsletters periodísticas españolas
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: Newsletters have re-emerged as a significant format in digital journalism, offering curated content in an era of information overload. While existing research has explored content curation on social media and by audiences, less attention has been paid to how news organizations themselves curate content in newsletters. This study addresses that gap by analyzing the curation practices of 84 newsletters from 16 major Spanish media outlets. Using an evaluative content analysis framework across two dimensions—Content and Curation—it examines aspects such as source diversity, time range, use of external content, sense-making techniques, and authorship. The authors aim to characterize the state of journalistic curation in Spain and identify best practices. Their main contribution is the identification of two distinct types of curation: intellectual and automated.

title: Hacia un nuevo canon televisivo: La historia reciente de la ficción española creada para el VOD (2016-2020)
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: The rise of VOD platforms has transformed television fiction globally, yet little is known about how Spanish productions within this space have developed distinctive production patterns. While prior research has addressed the business and technological dimensions of streaming, there is limited understanding of the formal and narrative norms shaping locally produced Spanish content. This study fills that gap by analyzing 60 Spanish series produced for major VOD platforms from 2016 to 2020. Using a mixed-methods approach, it identifies recurring formats, genres, and narrative structures to determine if a 'productive canon' has emerged. The paper contributes an empirically grounded periodization of Spanish VOD fiction and offers a descriptive framework for understanding its evolution.

title: Desinformación y vacunas en redes: Comportamiento de los bulos en Twitter
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: Anti-vaccine disinformation on social networks poses serious public health risks, and although prior research has examined hoax typologies and denialist discourse, less is known about the behavioral patterns of the users who propagate or counter such content. This study addresses that gap by analyzing the characteristics of Twitter accounts involved in spreading or refuting anti-vaccine hoaxes during the pandemic. Using a sample of 36,292 tweets identified via fact-checkers and filtered through Natural Language Inference, the authors analyze user metrics to determine if account morphology predicts dissemination behavior. The research question is whether features like follower count, verification, content volume, or account age influence how disinformation about vaccines spreads. They find that certain account types, such as those with more followers or verification, exhibit distinct patterns in content creation and retweeting, contributing to a predictive behavioral model.

title: La Moncloa en Twitter: un análisis cuantitativo en la era post COVID
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: The study addresses how the Spanish Government communicates on Twitter during a period of social, political, and economic uncertainty following the acute phase of the pandemic. While Twitter has been recognized as a key tool for institutional transparency and public engagement, there is limited understanding of whether governments align their digital communication strategies with both public interests and global recovery guidelines (such as those from the WHO and WEF). The research investigates whether the Spanish Government's tweets reflect citizen priorities or deviate from them, and whether they leverage Twitter’s interactive potential. Using a quantitative content analysis of 2,735 tweets, the study evaluates thematic focus, tone, format, timing, and engagement. The authors claim the work contributes to understanding institutional digital communication in times of crisis and identifies gaps between official messaging and public expectations.

title: La comedia cinematográfica aragonesa contemporánea. Claves creativas de sus cineastas y productores/as
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: Comedy is one of the most popular film genres and serves as a lens to reflect cultural identity and social issues, yet there is limited research on regional comedy in Spain, particularly Aragonese cinema. While existing studies highlight regional humor in places like Catalonia and the Basque Country, Aragon's cinematic comedy remains understudied. This research fills that gap by analyzing seven comedies funded by the Aragonese public broadcaster between 2013 and 2022. Through interviews with directors and producers, it investigates how creative decisions, cultural identity, and regional financing interact. The study specifically asks whether Aragonese comedy has distinctive features linked to 'somarda' humor—characterized by irony and subtlety—and how public funding influences its development. This contributes to a deeper understanding of peripheral cinema in Spain.

title: Compromiso con la Responsabilidad Social Corporativa. Un análisis de su visualización por parte de las agencias de relaciones públicas.
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: Public relations (PR) agencies play a central role in shaping how organizations communicate their Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) efforts, especially in the context of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). While CSR communication is increasingly strategic in the PR field, there remains a gap in understanding whether PR agencies themselves visibly offer specialized CSR services and whether they practice what they preach through their own CSR initiatives. Existing research focuses on CSR communication by corporations, but rarely examines the PR agencies promoting it. This study addresses that gap by analyzing the websites of 50 top PR agencies in Spain. The research asks: do these agencies offer CSR communication services, what types of CSR campaigns do they run for clients, do they have specialized professionals, and do they engage in their own CSR actions? The analysis uses a content analysis framework to evaluate both external client campaigns and internal agency actions. The main contribution lies in providing empirical evidence on the alignment between PR agencies’ professional offerings and their organizational behavior, highlighting a disconnect between external promotion and internal practice.

title: Redes sociales y tercer sector: análisis del uso de Facebook e Instagram en 50 ONG de España y Chile
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: NGOs in Spain and Chile play a significant role in social welfare and public action, yet their communication strategies on social media remain understudied. While existing research highlights the potential of social media for dialogue and engagement, little is known about how NGOs in different national contexts actually use platforms like Facebook and Instagram. This study addresses this gap by analyzing 2,103 posts from 50 NGOs (25 in each country) to understand their communication practices. The research questions focus on how NGOs use these platforms, differences in content and engagement between countries, and whether their communication is dialogic or purely informational. Using quantitative content analysis, the study examines publication formats, topics, tone, and interaction patterns. The main contribution is a comparative understanding of NGO digital communication in two Spanish-speaking countries, highlighting current limitations in strategic and interactive use.

title: Representaciones del conflicto armado en el cine colombiano
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: The armed conflict in Colombia, involving state forces and outlawed armed groups, has persisted for over fifty years and influenced various cultural expressions. Despite its centrality in national life, there is limited understanding of how Colombian cinema—as a key medium of representation—has depicted this conflict. Existing research has not systematically analyzed cinematic narratives about the conflict, especially from a structural narrative perspective. This study fills that gap by analyzing 14 Colombian feature films that engage with the armed conflict. Using a structuralist narrative approach, it investigates recurring themes, genres, spatiotemporal constructions, and character portrayals. The research contributes a descriptive mapping of how the conflict is framed in national cinema, highlighting tendencies toward fragmentation, pessimism, and indirect representation.

title: ¿Condiciona la imagen del país nuestras compras? Análisis clúster desde la perspectiva ciudadana
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: This study addresses the gap in country image research by focusing on internal perceptions within a nation, specifically how Ecuadorians' views of their country shape their consumption of national brands. While most prior research has analyzed country image from an external, international perspective, little attention has been paid to how citizens within a country—especially in emerging economies—differ in their perceptions based on sociodemographic characteristics. This study fills that gap by identifying distinct citizen segments through cluster analysis and examining how each group evaluates national brands. Using a survey of 823 Ecuadorian citizens and a two-step cluster analysis, the research identifies four sociodemographic segments and analyzes their assessments across six country image dimensions. Its contribution lies in demonstrating the heterogeneity of internal country image perceptions and linking them to consumer preferences, providing actionable insights for national branding strategies.

title: Las elecciones presidenciales de Estados Unidos de 2024: La desinformación desmentida por las verificadoras españolas
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: The 2024 U.S. presidential election generated significant international attention and became a focal point for disinformation, including in countries outside the U.S. such as Spain. While existing research has examined disinformation in domestic U.S. contexts, less is known about how foreign audiences receive and circulate false narratives about American elections. Spanish fact-checking platforms actively monitored and debunked such content, offering a unique dataset to study cross-border disinformation flows. This research investigates the formal characteristics, themes, sources, and dissemination channels of these falsehoods. Using content analysis of 204 fact-checks from five IFCN-verified Spanish platforms, it explores how disinformation about a foreign election is structured and propagated. The study contributes to understanding the transnational dimensions of electoral disinformation and the evolving role of AI in hoax production.

title: Percepción del papel de las Film commissions  y Film offices en la dinamización territorial: estrategias y retos para la promoción turística  en España
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: Audiovisual productions have increasingly influenced tourism, transforming filming locations into tourist destinations—a phenomenon known as screen tourism. While existing research highlights the economic and cultural impacts of this relationship, less is known about the role of intermediary institutions like film commissions and offices in shaping these outcomes. In Spain, these entities act as key facilitators between the audiovisual industry and regional governments, yet their specific strategies, contributions, and operational challenges remain underexplored. This research investigates how film commissions and offices in Spain perceive their role in territorial revitalization and tourism promotion. Using qualitative interviews with professionals from 25 different regional offices, the study analyzes their strategies, impacts, and obstacles. The findings aim to clarify how institutional support structures influence regional development through film-induced tourism.

title: ¿Hablar de publi me hace reconocerla mejor? Incidencia de la mediación parental y social en la alfabetización publicitaria de la generación Alpha
journal: The Revista Latina de Comunicación Social
rq_with_context: Children in Generation Alpha are increasingly exposed to sophisticated digital advertising, including influencer content and advergames, which are often hard to identify. This raises concerns about their ability to recognize persuasive intent and develop critical awareness. While prior research highlights the importance of advertising literacy, there is limited understanding of how social interactions—particularly with parents and peers—affect children’s abilities in this domain. This study addresses that gap by analyzing how parental and social mediation relate to children’s knowledge of advertising, their perceived ability to recognize it, and their sense of control over it. Using survey data from 1,304 Spanish children aged 7–10, the research employs correlational analysis to test five research questions. The findings contribute by showing that talking about advertising with parents positively affects both knowledge and recognition, while peer discussions have a weaker impact, and both types of interaction relate to perceived control.
